items.prompt: In a notification preferences system, a notification gateway must deliver a user notification. a slow provider must not consume all request capacity The design review focuses on cache placement and ownership across client, edge, service, and database layers. The normal path is healthy and the design must show where the decision belongs. What is the best primary architecture decision?
constraints: a slow provider must not consume all request capacity
Choose the mechanism that directly satisfies the stated contract before adding adjacent controls.
The primary decision is place a cache where its owner can state freshness, invalidation, and failure behavior..
Keep the scenario provider-neutral and do not rely on a canonical product solution.

options.text: Place a cache where its owner can state freshness, invalidation, and failure behavior. In this normal path for notification preferences, cache placement changes the consistency boundary and who can observe or repair stale data. The owner must also make a dependency that times out intermittently observable rather than silently passing it to another layer.

Choose the nearest familiar component and let each caller decide cache placement and ownership across client, edge, service, and database layers independently, without a shared owner or failure contract.
Add replication, caching, retries, or asynchronous buffering immediately, even though the scenario has not shown that mechanism is the limiting constraint.
Keep the happy path and treat a dependency that times out intermittently as an operational exception that the caller can resolve manually.
Select a named cloud or vendor product first and infer the workload, ownership, and guarantee from that product's defaults.

feedback.Reason: Place a cache where its owner can state freshness, invalidation, and failure behavior. It addresses a slow provider must not consume all request capacity through an explicit mechanism and keeps a dependency that times out intermittently inside a visible ownership and recovery boundary.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Cache placement changes the consistency boundary and who can observe or repair stale data. The applicability case makes the enforcement point explicit instead of relying on a product default.
Details.scenarioApplication: For notification preferences, the decision keeps a slow provider must not consume all request capacity attached to the owner that can observe the state. The design treats a dependency that times out intermittently as a named failure path.
Details.errorCorrection: The distractors either make the boundary unowned, add unmeasured complexity, ignore recovery, or replace mechanism reasoning with provider trivia. Choose the mechanism that directly satisfies the stated contract before adding adjacent controls.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Do not reduce “Cache placement and ownership across client, edge, service, and database layers” to terminology recall. Caching is a consistency decision, not a universal speed switch; distinguish authoritative data, derived views, and disposable acceleration layers. The trade-off is that explicit ownership and evidence may require a narrower contract or an operational signal, but that cost is preferable to silently violating the stated guarantee.
Details.ownership: The service or boundary that owns the relevant state and can enforce cache placement and ownership across client, edge, service, and database layers must own the decision; callers coordinate through the contract.
Details.transfer: Carry the ownership and failure rule into a new domain, then re-check the changed workload, guarantee, and recovery requirement.
Details.provenance: Technical claim anchored to RFC 9111 — HTTP Caching (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html); scenario, options, and feedback are independently authored.
